nameStory: Round-fruited rosette-panicgrass gets its name from two key features: its perfectly round seeds that feel like tiny BBs when you roll them between your fingers, and the distinctive rosette of leaves that spreads flat against the ground in fall and winter. The 'panic' part comes from 'panicle,' the loose, branching cluster of flowers that tops the grass stems.
description: Round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is a native perennial grass that grows in small clumps, typically reaching 1-3 feet tall during its growing season. Like other rosette grasses, it has a unique two-season growth pattern: upright flowering stems in summer, then a completely different flat rosette of broader leaves in fall and winter. This modest grass produces airy clusters of tiny flowers that mature into distinctive round seeds, and it's become quite rare in some parts of New England.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Perfectly round, bead-like seeds that feel smooth and hard when rolled between your fingers - they're noticeably more spherical than the oval seeds of most other grasses

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dramatic seasonal transformation from upright summer stems to flat winter rosettes of completely different-looking leaves pressed against the ground

idTips.label: Summer Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth to slightly rough, typically 2-4 inches long and arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Winter Rosette
idTips.description: Broad, oval leaves arranged in a flat circle against the ground, feeling softer and more papery than the summer leaves

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Delicate, open clusters of tiny purplish or greenish flowers that create an airy, cloud-like appearance at the top of stems

habitat: Look for round-fruited rosette-panicgrass in dry, sandy or rocky soils in open woodlands, clearings, and woodland edges. It prefers acidic soils and partial shade, often growing alongside other native grasses and wildflowers in areas that aren't too heavily disturbed. In New England, it's most likely found in oak-pine forests and their margins.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as narrow, upright stems with small leaves, beginning the summer phase of this grass's dual personality.
seasonality.summer: Produces its characteristic airy flower clusters and develops the round seeds that give it its name - this is when it's tallest and most visible.
seasonality.fall: The upright stems die back while completely different rosette leaves emerge, creating flat circles of broad, soft leaves pressed to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Persists as distinctive flat rosettes of broad leaves that remain green under snow, looking nothing like the summer grass form.

funFact: This grass is like a botanical shape-shifter - if you saw the summer and winter forms side by side, you'd swear they were completely different species! The transformation is so dramatic that early botanists actually classified the two seasonal forms as separate plants.
confusionNotes: The round seeds are your best bet for identification since many rosette grasses look similar. Other Dichanthelium species have oval or pointed seeds - if you can roll a perfectly round seed like a tiny marble, you've likely found round-fruited rosette-panicgrass.
contextualKnowledge: This species is considered endangered in Michigan and of special concern in Connecticut, making it a conservation priority. The name 'panic grass' has nothing to do with panic or fear - it comes from the Latin 'panicum,' an ancient name for millet and related grasses.
compareHints: Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds. The winter rosettes tend to be more compact and the leaves broader than many of its cousins, but the round seeds are the most reliable distinguishing feature.

Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
